title: Special Education: Orthopraxy
author: Sancho, Norma
summary: Parents know it, teachers know it, heaven knows it: there are physical conditions that require direct clinical attention. Fractures, infections, sensory impairments, injuries, neurological damage you can actually see and measure and point to. In these cases, the language we use tends to stay relatively honest, because the thing we are describing pushes back. It has edges. It resists interpretation. Now think back to your own years in school. You probably remember at least one of them, the kid who couldn't quite get reading, no matter how many times the teacher went over it. The one whose handwriting was, somehow, always a disaster (and also, almost certainly, the one whose handwriting was so beautiful it made everyone else quietly furious, which I am fairly sure was my brother in Utah). The one who froze every time numbers appeared on the board. The one who never raised their hand, ever, or the one who couldn't seem to stop raising it. The one who sat in the back and looked out the window. The one who talked back. The one teachers described, in hushed tones in the hallway, as "a lot to handle." You remember them. You might even have been one of them. This article is not a retrospective. Kids like those are still in classrooms, and the system that receives them and hands them back with a label has not changed as much as it likes to believe. So, we will no talk about the fractures or the infections, but what happens when the thing being described is something considerably harder to pin down: the way a person thinks, learns, moves through the world, responds to authority, processes language, tolerates boredom, or decides, consciously or not, that a particular classroom is not a place where they belong. The problem is that once we leave the body and enter what we broadly call "the mind," the language we use stops behaving itself. Mental processes are not like bones. They are more like fingerprints: structurally comparable across people, but infinitely variable in pattern, rhythm, intensity, and response to context. There is no standard fingerprint. There is no standard mind either, only minds shaped by temperament, biography, language, relational history, cultural norms, material conditions, and the particular circumstances in which a person has had to survive, adapt, and make meaning. When the distinction blurs, description stops staying descriptive. Behavior becomes identity. Action becomes trait. Trait becomes defect. What began as observation ends as classification. Language meant to describe behavior constructs identity, and the tool it reaches for, almost every time, is a category. Classification does not enter as understanding but as a way of managing uncertainty by assigning people to boxes. And in education, few hands have been more eager to hold the stamp than the teacher's. Mysteries of Literacy First Mystery: The Inconclusive Career of a Word. The term "dyslexia" has been around for over a hundred and thirty years, which is long enough, you would think, to have arrived somewhere definitive. It has not. To this day, researchers continue to debate how to define it, how to diagnose it, and how best to teach reading to the children it is supposed to describe. Not a minor footnote but the headline. Let's see, then, how we got here, because the history of how scientists have tried to explain dyslexia is itself a kind of story, and not an entirely flattering one. The earliest theories looked at children who could not read and concluded, reasonably enough, that something in the brain must be responsible. From there, the field spent decades trying to locate the problem: first in structural damage, then in functional damage, then in something delightfully named "Minimal Brain Dysfunction," which deserves a moment of our attention. Minimal Brain Dysfunction was the explanation offered for cases where no actual brain damage could be found. The logic went roughly like this: the child cannot read; reading is a brain function; therefore, there must be something wrong with the brain, even if we cannot see it, measure it, or point to it. The damage was inferred from the very behavior it was supposed to explain. If you find that circular, you are in good company. Specialists in the field have noted it themselves: it falls into tautology. A child has dyslexia because of minimal brain dysfunction, and we know there is minimal brain dysfunction because the child has dyslexia. The snake eats its tail, publishes its findings, and gets cited. Entire empires of prestige were raised upon such intellectual trifles. But this did not stop the theories from multiplying. Hinshelwood, Orton, Strauss, Lehtinen, Cruickshank, Myklebust et al. each arrived with a new explanation, each one slightly different from the last, each one confident. Bakker proposed two types of dyslexia based on which hemisphere was doing too much work and when. Rourke identified a non-verbal learning disability linked to the right hemisphere and spent considerable effort mapping its consequences. Obrutz and colleagues argued the problem was not in either hemisphere alone but in the communication between them, mediated by the corpus callosum, which in some children fails to properly inhibit signals from one side, causing interference. Then came the genetic theories. If the problem was not visible in the brain, perhaps it was written into the DNA. Hallgren studied hundreds of dyslexic families. Hermann compared identical and fraternal twins. Decker, DeFries, Plomin, Pennington, Raskind and others all found correlations between reading difficulties and family history, which sounds definitive until you remember that families also share homes, habits, bookshelves, dinner table conversations, and attitudes toward school. Separating the genetic signal from the environmental noise turned out to be harder than expected. Then came the biochemical theories. Feingold proposed in 1975 that sensitivity to salicylates, a chemical compound found in certain artificial colorings and in some perfectly ordinary foods like apples, oranges, tomatoes, cucumbers, and tea, could cause hyperactivity and learning difficulties. He reported a fifty percent success rate with salicylate-free diets, which is the kind of number that sounds impressive until you start asking inconvenient questions. Like: what exactly were these children eating before? Did the structure itself, the routine, the care, the fact that somebody was finally watching, account for something? Feingold saw improvement and went straight to the salicylates. The possibility that the children were simply, for once, eating regularly and being noticed does not appear to have made it into the methodology. It was, in spirit, not entirely unlike what we now call a keto diet: one looks to shrink a stubborn belly, the other to reduce a supposed inflammation, and both work just enough of the time to keep the theory alive and the book sales going. Each of these models was internally coherent, and each also has been questioned, refuted, or found to explain only a subset of the children. The brain scan studies found structural differences in dyslexic children but could not fully replicate results or rule out other variables. The postmortem studies found cytoarchitectural anomalies but could not be generalized. The genetic studies found family patterns that suggested heritability but could not separate genetic transmission from shared environment, shared habits, and the simple fact that if your parent struggled to read, you probably grew up in a house with fewer books and less reading aloud at bedtime. None of this means the research is worthless. It is not. Some children do have neurological differences that meaningfully affect how they process written language. The question is not whether dyslexia exists but what counts as understanding it. For the case, what is striking is not the theory but the relentless confidence. Each one arrives certain enough to name and classify; to build a taxonomy, to found a school of thought, a new stigma. The hunger, whether for answers or for authorship, is a powerful thing. Across more than a century of competing frameworks, the option of simply saying "we do not know yet" seems never to have been seriously entertained. It does not get you tenure. The current picture is not much tidier. There is now broad support for what researchers call a "multifactorial basis," meaning that multiple causes are probably involved, including phonological difficulties, oral language limitations, processing speed, and even environmental factors like poverty and trauma. The subtypes are still being mapped: a 2024 study identified three distinct neurocognitive subtypes in children with dyslexia, while other researchers propose different groupings based on different criteria, in different languages, with different results. As for whether it can be overcome: children who become capable readers have not outgrown their dyslexia but learned mental workarounds, their brains using different pathways than non-dyslexic readers. Which raises the quiet but important question of whether "dyslexia" describes a fixed condition, an adaptive difference, or simply one end of a very wide spectrum of how human brains learn to read. No one is quite sure. But everyone has a category for it. Currently, "dyslexia" does not exist as a standalone diagnosis in the DSM-5, the Malleus Maleficarum of mental health. It has been absorbed into a broader category called Specific Learning Disorder, with the specifier "impairment in reading" added when the difficulty involves word recognition, fluency, or comprehension. Second Mystery: The Tongue as a Problem Stuttering is older than medicine. It is likely as old as speech itself and appears in every social group across recorded history. Which means humanity has had a very long time to come up with explanations for it, and has used that time with characteristic confidence and very mixed results. In ancient Greece, Hippocrates wrote that stuttering resulted from dryness of the tongue. His solution was to blister it. Not metaphorically. First-century Roman physician Celsus recommended that the patient immerse his head in cold water, eat horseradish, and vomit, and was also an early advocate of surgery to detach the ligament under the tongue. The logic, across centuries, was remarkably consistent: the tongue is the problem, so the tongue must be corrected, reshaped, reduced, or in some cases partially removed. In the 1840s, a Prussian surgeon named Dieffenbach came up with what he called a radical cure, an incision through the root of the tongue that he claimed stopped the spasm of the vocal chords. He performed this without anesthesia. Perhaps, one historian noted, his patients stopped stuttering because they passed out. Then came the twentieth century, which decided the tongue was not the problem at all. The problem was the mother. NORMA SANCHO - THE HUMAN CURRICULUM is a reader-supported publication. Wendell Johnson, a speech pathologist at the University of Iowa, proposed what he called the diagnosogenic theory: that stuttering does not begin as a neurological or physiological abnormality. It begins, he wrote, not in the child's mouth but in the parent's ear. His argument was that anxious parents hear their child's normal speech disfluencies, label them as stuttering, correct and worry and hover, and in doing so teach the child to be afraid of their own voice. The diagnosis, in other words, creates the disorder. It was an interesting idea. It also led to one of the more disturbing experiments in speech science. In 1939, Johnson and his graduate student Mary Tudor took twenty-two orphans and spent four months systematically telling the normally fluent ones that they were stutterers, to see if the label alone could produce the condition. It was called, by those who found out about it decades later, the Monster Study. The children were not told it was an experiment. Some of them carried speech problems for the rest of their lives. Johnson's theory eventually fell out of favor, in part because subsequent studies found that children who received a diagnosis of stuttering commonly had abnormally high levels of disfluency before anyone diagnosed them, which suggested that in most cases the parental concern was not the origin of the problem but a response to something already there.11 The mother, it turned out, was probably not inventing it. More recent research has located a specific brain network responsible for stuttering, and the current understanding is that it is a brain disorder related to the regulation of speech production, with genetic components that researchers are still mapping. So: not the tongue, not the mother, probably the brain, possibly the genes, still being worked out. What is also known is that sixty to seventy percent of children who stutter are clear by adolescence, and around eighty percent by adulthood,13 which raises its own set of uncomfortable questions. If it resolves that often without intervention, what exactly were all those tongue surgeries and horseradish treatments and orphan experiments for? And more quietly: if most children simply stop, what does that tell us about what was happening in the first place? Here is what the research does say, and what I find genuinely worth sitting with: many experts today attribute chronic stuttering to the speaker's efforts to avoid painful emotions created by their own evaluations of stuttering: fear of guilt, fear of shame, fear of fear itself. The attempts to avoid these feelings result in efforts to avoid stuttering, and those efforts make things worse. So, what keeps stuttering chronic, in many cases, is the anticipation of judgment, which brings me to the question I keep circling: what if the most honest explanation for why some children cannot get their words out smoothly in certain rooms, in front of certain people, under certain kinds of scrutiny, is also the simplest one? What if it is fear? Fear of what, exactly? Of mockery? Of being ridiculed? Probably of being heard wrong, of the pause being filled by someone else before the sentence is finished. Then, what kind of place are we asking these children to speak in, and what have we taught them to expect when they do? Currently, or more precisely, officially, "stuttering" no longer exists as a diagnosis in the DSM-5, the Malleus Maleficarum of mental health. It has been renamed Childhood-Onset Fluency Disorder. Dr. Gerald Maguire, a consultant for the DSM revision, says it plainly: "for many people, this is what can disable them. They may have a high level of anxiety and they avoid certain speaking situations or certain words and they focus so much of the time around the avoidance and the anxiety." In other words, the most influential manual in mental health ends up suggesting that what truly paralyzes the person who stutters is the fear of stuttering. Which is exactly what we said. We just did not need a manual to say it. Third Mystery: Reading Everything and Understood Nothing There is a condition that almost nobody talks about, which is interesting given that it sits at the exact center of what schools claim to care about most in this technological era. It is called hyperlexia, and it is, in the most literal sense, the mirror image of dyslexia. A child with hyperlexia begins reading words remarkably earlier than expected for their age. They can decode and identify letters and words with impressive fluency. What they cannot do, or cannot do reliably, is understand what they are reading. The mechanism works but the meaning does not arrive. Hyperlexia is defined as the co-occurrence of advanced reading skills relative to comprehension, the early acquisition of reading without explicit teaching, and a strong orientation toward written material, generally in the context of a neurodevelopmental disorder. It was first identified in 1967, which means it has been known about for nearly sixty years, and it remains one of the least studied, least discussed, and least diagnosed conditions in the entire landscape of learning differences. There is no century-long argument about it. There is barely a conversation. This is worth pausing on. We have spent over a hundred and thirty years debating, theorizing, naming, cutting, medicating, and redesigning curricula around the child who cannot decode text. The child who can decode everything but understands nothing has been more or less left to the footnotes. One possible reason for this is that hyperlexia does not look like a problem from the outside because the child reads. The child reads well, early and eagerly and often. That looks, to any reasonable teacher or parent, like exactly what school is supposed to produce. The alarm does not sound because the performance is convincing. Probably until it is election time. Many of our currents educational and social problems seems to scream the same fact: We have consistently measured the wrong thing. Data from national assessments in the United States revealed that reading comprehension outcomes have worsened nationwide, with more students scoring below proficiency in 2024 than in 2022 or 2019. A full forty percent of fourth graders scored below basic in reading comprehension in 2024, representing approximately 1.4 million children. These are not children who cannot decode. Many of them can decode perfectly well. What they cannot do is make meaning from what they read, which is, one might argue, the entire point of the exercise. Some of those children, sitting through year after year of school knowing they are not getting it, choose to act out, to withdraw anxiously, to cheat elaborately, to leave altogether, because those things provide a shield from the slowly unspooling experience of being the kid who never got it. They get classified. They get labeled. They get sent somewhere. And the question of what they were actually struggling to understand, and why, and in what language, and under what conditions, tends not to make it into the report. Hyperlexia, in this sense, is not just a clinical curiosity. It is a kind of parable. It tells us that fluency and comprehension are not the same thing, that performance and understanding are not the same thing, and that a child who produces exactly what the system is looking for may still be, underneath that performance, quite lost. That question is not simple: when we teach a child to read, what exactly are we teaching them to do? To decode symbols? To produce correct answers about texts? To participate in a particular kind of language that school considers legitimate? And if a child can do all of that without understanding any of it, what have we actually taught them? That question, it turns out, is not really about reading at all. It is about what school is for, who it is designed to serve, and what happens to the children for whom the performance and the understanding never quite connect. Which is, not coincidentally, exactly where this article is headed next. Currently, hyperlexia has no clear definition in the DSM-5 either. It is listed as part of autism spectrum disorder, which means that a child who reads everything and understands nothing does not get a condition of their own. They get absorbed into a spectrum. Researchers do not know the exact cause of hyperlexia, and there is no specific test to diagnose it. Three mysteries, three sections of the DSM-5, three different ways of saying: we are still working on it. The manual, however, looks very confident. Witch Children: Misconduct and the Courts. Each of these children arrived at school carrying with them what they had learned at home, the only place a child learns anything before the age of five. Others were given chaos, silence, fear, or love expressed in ways no one would call love.

And the system functions because the alternative, stepping outside the role, insisting on being a private person rather than a public symbol, would unravel something much larger than any one person's comfort. And the child, sitting across from either of them, is not meeting a person, they are meeting an institution.

That the diagnostic manuals are revised every few years, adding and removing conditions with a frequency that does not suggest settled knowledge so much as ongoing negotiation. That a child can receive four different diagnoses from four different clinicians looking at the same behavior.
